A_target.statement:
Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a [[Definition:Measure Space|measure space]].
Let $\sequence {f_n}$ be [[Definition:Measurable Function|measurable functions]] with $f_n \to f$ [[Definition:Pointwise Convergence|pointwise]].
Let $g$ be [[Definition:Integrable Function|integrable]] with $\size {f_n} \le g$ for all $n$.
Then:
:$\displaystyle \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \int f_n \rd \mu = \int f \rd \mu$

B_source.statement:
Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a [[Definition:Finite Measure Space|finite measure space]].
Let $\size {f_n} \le M$ with $f_n \to f$ [[Definition:Pointwise Convergence|pointwise]].
Then:
:$\displaystyle \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \int f_n \rd \mu = \int f \rd \mu$

derived.convergence of the integrals: the same conclusion, now without finiteness of the measure
derived.the constant M being integrable on a fin: integrability of g as the correct replacement hypothesis

object_map.reformulation: Replace the constant bound on a finite measure space by an integrable envelope, which is what the argument actually requires.

validity_conditions: On a finite measure space a constant is integrable, so the bounded convergence theorem is exactly the special case g = M and the generalization is faithful.
Integrability of the dominating function, not its boundedness, is what the proof actually uses, via Fatou applied to g + f_n and g - f_n.
Some dominating hypothesis is necessary: without it pointwise convergence alone does not force convergence of the integrals, as escaping-mass examples show.
proof_plan: Replace the constant bound $M$ on a finite measure space by the [[Definition:Integrable Function|integrable]] dominating function $g$.

Subtracting the finite quantity $\displaystyle \int g \rd \mu$:
:$\displaystyle \limsup_{n \mathop \to \infty} \int f_n \rd \mu \le \int f \rd \mu \le \liminf_{n \mathop \to \infty} \int f_n \rd \mu$
